Move-in is more than a key handoff. It’s a chance to make the essentials easy to find later.

A brief from Stewards of Affordable Housing for the Future’s Housing Stability Cohort shares examples of lease-up materials in plain language and resident welcome kits with practical information.

If you were editing a one-page move-in guide, what would you put first: key contacts, essential community procedures, or where to ask for help?

Source: SAHF, “Resident Communication Touchpoints” (PDF): https://sahfnet.org/sites/default/files/documents/sahf-resident-communication-touchpoints-brief.pdf

Illustrative scene created with AI.

Resident communication doesn’t stop after move-in. The question is whether residents can still access and understand information when they need it.

SAHF’s Resident Communication Touchpoints brief recommends considering barriers such as language, literacy, unreliable internet, and difficulty leaving home—and using clear language, translation, or visuals where appropriate.

A useful review prompt for any recurring resident message: Who might have trouble accessing or understanding this, and what alternative would help?

Source: SAHF, “Resident Communication Touchpoints Brief” (accessed 2026-10-04): https://sahfnet.org/sites/default/files/documents/sahf-resident-communication-touchpoints-brief.pdf

Illustrative scene created with AI.

Energy goals are easier to carry into daily work when they’re part of the welcome.

For multifamily teams, one practical starting point is to include a short energy-management primer in employee onboarding: explain the organization’s environmental priorities, then connect each role to relevant day-to-day practices. ENERGY STAR also suggests education for facilities teams on how their responsibilities can support energy-management efforts.

That’s a communication practice, not a claim of measured savings. Start with a clear goal, role-specific examples, and a way for new staff to ask questions.

Source: ENERGY STAR, “Improving Multifamily Energy Management Through Stakeholder Engagement” (August 2021; accessed 2026-10-04): https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/tools/ENERGYSTARMultifamilyStakeholderEngagement_10_2021.pdf

Illustrative scene created with AI.

Good indoor-air-quality communication shouldn’t start and end with a complaint.

EPA’s building guidance recommends sharing accurate information, clarifying responsibilities among management, staff, occupants, and contractors, and establishing a way to log and respond to complaints.

For a multifamily team, a practical starting point is to make clear where residents can raise a concern and who will follow up. Adapt the approach to the building and its occupants.

Source: U.S. EPA, “Building Air Quality” — “Effective Communication” section (accessed 2026-10-04): https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2014-08/documents/sec_3.pdf

Illustrative scene created with AI.

A late-rent notice can be both clear about the situation and clear about what a resident can do next.

SAHF’s Resident Communication Touchpoints brief describes examples that include contact information for management or resident-services staff, possible repayment-plan information if available, and ways to look for rental assistance. The point is not to promise a particular option—it’s to make the available next step easy to find.

Source: SAHF, “Resident Communication Touchpoints Brief” (accessed 2026-10-04): https://sahfnet.org/sites/default/files/documents/sahf-resident-communication-touchpoints-brief.pdf

Illustrative scene created with AI.

“Use less energy” is a message. A shared goal, a relevant update, and a practical next step make it more useful.

ENERGY STAR’s tenant-engagement guidance recommends sharing energy-efficiency goals and data with occupants, tailoring messages to the audience, and offering specific actions people can take. A property newsletter or lobby update could explain the goal and invite residents to share suggestions.

Keep the distinction clear: report measured progress only when you have data to support it. A goal is not a result.

Source: ENERGY STAR, “8 Great Strategies to Engage Tenants on Energy Efficiency” (accessed 2026-10-04): https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/buildings/tools/8-Great-Strategies-to-Engage-Tenants.pdf

Illustrative scene created with AI.

A building-wide waste routine needs more than bins; it needs clear ownership and a way to see what is changing.

EPA recommends involving people from different departments, tenants, or functions in waste-reduction planning. Its commercial-buildings guide also points to setting goals and tracking waste as foundations for a program.

A practical first step: invite the people who touch purchasing, resident communication, and day-to-day operations to help choose one measurable goal. What’s useful will depend on the building and its waste services.

Source: U.S. EPA, “Managing and Reducing Wastes: A Guide for Commercial Buildings” (accessed 2026-10-04): https://www.epa.gov/smm/managing-and-reducing-wastes-guide-commercial-buildings

Illustrative scene created with AI.

Energy-related work can cross organizational lines. ENERGY STAR’s multifamily stakeholder guide suggests collaborative events and competitions as ways to engage staff; it also describes involving property teams in energy treasure hunts. The guide separately suggests recognizing staff contributions through options such as a company announcement or employee award.

A practical discussion prompt for your team: how do you make cross-functional contributions visible and appreciated?

Source: ENERGY STAR, “Improving Multifamily Energy Management Through Stakeholder Engagement” (August 2021; accessed 2026-10-04): https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/tools/ENERGYSTARMultifamilyStakeholderEngagement_10_2021.pdf

A useful resident-feedback loop does not end when someone submits a comment. Close it by letting residents know their input was taken seriously and how it was considered; without follow-up, people may stop contributing. Even when a suggestion cannot be adopted, a clear response can make the process feel real rather than performative. What is one simple way your team closes the loop after a resident shares an idea?

Source: Chapter Four: Working with Residents (accessed 2026-10-17): https://www.hud.gov/sites/documents/43815c4hsgh.pdf

Illustrative scene created with AI.

Evacuation plans should account for how people will get where they need to go—not just which route they will take. Ready.gov advises planning ahead for accessible transportation that may be needed for evacuation or getting around during or after a disaster. For residents who may need that support, identifying options before an emergency is more practical than trying to arrange them under pressure. Consider including transportation needs in individual preparedness conversations.

Source: Personal Disaster Preparedness for People with Disabilities Social Media Toolkit | Ready.gov (accessed 2026-10-17): https://www.ready.gov/disability-toolkit

Emergency plans work better as practical instructions than as documents people only encounter during a drill. OSHA notes that the best emergency action plans include employees in the planning process, explain what employees should do in an emergency, and provide proper training. Inviting staff to help shape the plan can surface questions about real work routines before an incident. Which responsibilities or handoffs should your team make clearer in its next planning review?

Source: Develop & Implement an Emergency Action Plan (EAP) | OSHA (accessed 2026-10-17): https://www.osha.gov/etools/evacuation-plans-procedures/eap/develop-implement

Illustrative scene created with AI.

Multifamily integrated pest management is a shared operation. EPA describes an effective IPM team as including residents, maintenance and custodial staff, pest management professionals, and the housing manager. Those roles may notice different parts of a situation: a resident's observation, a custodial routine, a maintenance issue, or a professional assessment. A useful planning exercise is to map who contributes which information and who coordinates the next step. Which perspectives belong in your property's pest-management conversation?

Source: Pest Control: Resources for Housing Managers | US EPA (accessed 2026-10-17): https://www.epa.gov/safepestcontrol/pest-control-resources-housing-managers

Illustrative scene created with AI.

Shared waste areas have to serve the building’s actual needs. EPA describes contract approaches that can specify reuse, recycling, and composting services for multifamily customers, or set a minimum volume per dwelling unit to help ensure adequate capacity in shared-service settings. These are options to consider when reviewing service terms—not a universal rule. A practical contract conversation starts with what services residents can use and whether collection capacity fits the property.

Source: Best Practices: Equal Services for Multi-Family Customers | US EPA (accessed 2026-10-17): https://www.epa.gov/transforming-waste-tool/multi-family-customers

A power-outage checklist can begin with a simple inventory: what at home depends on electricity? Ready.gov suggests identifying those needs and planning for batteries or other alternative power sources, such as a portable charger or power bank. The useful details are personal: which devices matter to your household, how they are powered, and what backup options are available. Reviewing that list before an outage can help turn a vague concern into a concrete preparation task.

Source: Power Outages | Ready.gov (accessed 2026-10-17): https://www.ready.gov/power-outages

Illustrative scene created with AI.

Before choosing a waste intervention, understand what is actually in the waste stream. EPA defines a waste assessment or audit as a systematic review of a building and its operations to identify the quantity and composition of materials being discarded. That baseline can help teams ask more focused questions about local options instead of selecting a program first and hoping it fits. What would your building want to learn from an assessment before making its next waste-planning decision?

Source: Managing and Reducing Wastes: A Guide for Commercial Buildings | US EPA (accessed 2026-10-17): https://www.epa.gov/smm/managing-and-reducing-wastes-guide-commercial-buildings
